--- title: "Tracking Spending" --- ## Book Topics - **Tracking vs. budgeting**: tracking records where money actually went; budgeting allocates where it should go; comparing the two creates a feedback loop - **Capture methods**: spending journal, checkbook register, cash envelopes, bank statements; pick one and run it for a full month - **Categorizing**: start with about 10 stable buckets (housing, transportation, groceries, dining out, subscriptions, personal, health, gifts, fun money, other); when in doubt use "Other", and only promote a new category after seeing it three months in a row - **Using spreadsheets**: bank exports have `Date`, `Description`, and `Amount` columns; a keyword lookup adds the `Category` column in one pass - **Monthly review**: pull, categorize, compare to budget, and pick *one* change for next month - **Online subscriptions**: Americans spend about $219/month on subscriptions and underestimate it by $133; audit every quarter and cancel anything unused in 30 days - **Math**: the subscription audit, the opportunity cost of a $20/month subscription invested at 7% for 30 years (about $22,700) ## Bank Statement Data A minimal bank export has three columns: `Date`, `Description`, and `Amount`. The code blocks below show how to create an example bank statement file in R, Python, and Excel. ::: panel-tabset ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r_bank_statement <- tibble::tibble( Date = as.Date(c( "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06", "2026-01-07", "2026-01-08", "2026-01-09", "2026-01-10", "2026-01-11", "2026-01-12", "2026-01-13", "2026-01-14", "2026-01-15" )), Description = c( "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness" ), Amount = c( 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99 ) ) r_bank_statement |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Date |Description | Amount| |:----------|:--------------------|--------:| |2026-01-02 |Employer Payroll | 2400.00| |2026-01-02 |Rent | -1500.00| |2026-01-03 |Comcast Internet | -75.00| |2026-01-03 |Trader Joe's | -82.45| |2026-01-04 |Shell Gas | -45.20| |2026-01-04 |Netflix | -15.99| |2026-01-05 |Starbucks | -6.75| |2026-01-06 |PG&E Electric | -142.30| |2026-01-07 |AT&T Wireless | -85.00| |2026-01-08 |Spotify | -10.99| |2026-01-09 |Whole Foods | -64.12| |2026-01-10 |Chipotle | -14.50| |2026-01-11 |Geico Auto Insurance | -125.00| |2026-01-12 |NYTimes Digital | -17.00| |2026-01-13 |Shell Gas | -42.80| |2026-01-14 |Costco | -156.78| |2026-01-15 |24 Hour Fitness | -39.99| ::: ::: We can view the bank statement in R using `knitr::kable()`. ## Python In Python, we'll use `polars` to create a `DataFrame` and display the bank statement. This is similar to the `tibble` we created above. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import polars as pl py_bank_statement = pl.DataFrame({ "Date": [ "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-04", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06", "2026-01-07", "2026-01-08", "2026-01-09", "2026-01-10", "2026-01-11", "2026-01-12", "2026-01-13", "2026-01-14", "2026-01-15" ], "Description": [ "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's", "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric", "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle", "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco", "24 Hour Fitness" ], "Amount": [ 2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75, -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00, -42.80, -156.78, -39.99 ] }).with_columns(pl.col("Date").str.to_date()) py_bank_statement ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Excel We can simply copy and paste the data into Excel; `Date` in A, `Description` in B, `Amount` in C. ![`bank_statement` in Excel](img/tracking_spending-bank-statement.png){width='75%' fig-align='center'} ::: ## Categorizing Transactions Map description keywords to budget buckets in a single pass. ::: panel-tabset ## R In R, we can use `dplyr` to do the following: - `dplyr::case_when()` evaluates each pattern in order and assigns the matching category - `grepl()` does the keyword test against `Description` - The final `TRUE` arm catches everything that didn't match and labels it `"Other"` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r_bank_statement <- r_bank_statement |> dplyr::mutate( Category = dplyr::case_when( grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income", grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing", grepl("Comcast|PG&E|AT&T", Description) ~ "Utilities", grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries", grepl("Shell", Description) ~ "Transportation", grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining", grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions", grepl("Geico", Description) ~ "Insurance", TRUE ~ "Other" ) ) r_bank_statement |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Date |Description | Amount|Category | |:----------|:--------------------|--------:|:--------------| |2026-01-02 |Employer Payroll | 2400.00|Income | |2026-01-02 |Rent | -1500.00|Housing | |2026-01-03 |Comcast Internet | -75.00|Utilities | |2026-01-03 |Trader Joe's | -82.45|Groceries | |2026-01-04 |Shell Gas | -45.20|Transportation | |2026-01-04 |Netflix | -15.99|Subscriptions | |2026-01-05 |Starbucks | -6.75|Dining | |2026-01-06 |PG&E Electric | -142.30|Utilities | |2026-01-07 |AT&T Wireless | -85.00|Utilities | |2026-01-08 |Spotify | -10.99|Subscriptions | |2026-01-09 |Whole Foods | -64.12|Groceries | |2026-01-10 |Chipotle | -14.50|Dining | |2026-01-11 |Geico Auto Insurance | -125.00|Insurance | |2026-01-12 |NYTimes Digital | -17.00|Subscriptions | |2026-01-13 |Shell Gas | -42.80|Transportation | |2026-01-14 |Costco | -156.78|Groceries | |2026-01-15 |24 Hour Fitness | -39.99|Subscriptions | ::: ::: ## Python `polars` is similar to `dplyr`, but: - `with_columns()` is the `mutate()` analog - a chain of `pl.when().then()` calls is the `case_when()` analog - `pl.col("Description").str.contains(...)` does the keyword test - regex by default and the `|` between merchants is alternation ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} py_bank_statement = py_bank_statement.with_columns( Category = pl.when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Payroll")).then(pl.lit("Income")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Rent")).then(pl.lit("Housing")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Comcast|PG&E|AT&T")).then(pl.lit("Utilities")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco")).then(pl.lit("Groceries")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Shell")).then(pl.lit("Transportation")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")).then(pl.lit("Dining")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness")).then(pl.lit("Subscriptions")) .when(pl.col("Description").str.contains("Geico")).then(pl.lit("Insurance")) .otherwise(pl.lit("Other")) ) py_bank_statement ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Excel In Excel, the [`IFS()` function](https://support.microsoft.com/en-US/Excel/IFS-function) is the direct analog of `case_when()`/`when().then()`. - `IFS()` takes a list of conditions and corresponding values, evaluated top to bottom, with the first match winning - `SEARCH()` returns the position of a keyword in a cell (or `#VALUE!` if not found) - Wrapping it in `ISNUMBER()` turns that into a true/false test - For categories with several rows/transactions, wrap the tests in `OR()` - The final `TRUE, "Other"` arm is the equivalent of `dplyr`'s `TRUE ~ "Other"` and `polars`'s `.otherwise(...)`; it catches anything that didn't match an earlier pattern. ```swift =IFS( ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Payroll",B2)), "Income", ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Rent",B2)), "Housing", OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Comcast",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("PG&E",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("AT&T",B2))), "Utilities", OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Trader Joe",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Whole Foods",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Costco",B2))), "Groceries", ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Shell",B2)), "Transportation", OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Starbucks",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Chipotle",B2))), "Dining", OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Netflix",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Spotify",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("NYTimes",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("24 Hour Fitness",B2))), "Subscriptions", ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Geico",B2)), "Insurance", TRUE, "Other" ) ``` If the statement is laid out with `Date` in column `A`, `Description` in column `B`, and `Amount` in column `C`, type `Category` in cell `D1`, then paste the formula below into `D2`: ![`IFS()` in Excel](img/tracking_spending-ifs.png){width='100%' fig-align='center'} Then copy `D2` down through every transaction row (select `D2`, double-click the small square in the bottom-right corner, or use `Ctrl+D` after selecting `D2:D{last_row}`). * To add a new merchant when one shows up: edit the formula in `D2`, then re-fill down. Keep the new merchant near the bottom of its category group so the existing patterns still resolve first. In Excel, we can also use the *Format as Table* feature to make the data easier to read.[^excel-tables] You can select a color/style for your table and it will automatically update the data. ![Format as table](img/tracking_spending-format-as-table.png){width='100%' fig-align='center'} [^excel-tables]: Read the [Overview of Excel tables](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/overview-of-excel-tables) on the Microsoft documentation. ::: ## Answering Tracking Questions Once every row has a category, the book's three tracking questions take one short pipeline each: what did subscriptions cost, what share of income went to fixed costs, and which variable category was biggest? ::: panel-tabset ## R Totals by category, spending only (negative amounts), largest first: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} income <- sum(r_bank_statement$Amount[r_bank_statement$Amount > 0]) category_totals <- r_bank_statement |> dplyr::filter(Amount < 0) |> dplyr::group_by(Category) |> dplyr::summarise(Total = -sum(Amount), .groups = "drop") |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Total)) |> dplyr::mutate(Share = fmt_pct(Total / income)) category_totals |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Category | Total|Share | |:--------------|-------:|:-----| |Housing | 1500.00|62.5% | |Groceries | 303.35|12.6% | |Utilities | 302.30|12.6% | |Insurance | 125.00|5.2% | |Transportation | 88.00|3.7% | |Subscriptions | 83.97|3.5% | |Dining | 21.25|0.9% | ::: ::: Total spent on subscriptions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} category_totals$Total[category_totals$Category == "Subscriptions"] |> fmt_dollar() #> [1] "$83.97" ``` ::: Share of income going to fixed costs (housing, utilities, and insurance): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fixed <- c("Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance") fixed_total <- sum(category_totals$Total[category_totals$Category %in% fixed]) fmt_dollar(fixed_total) #> [1] "$1,927.30" fmt_pct(fixed_total / income) #> [1] "80.3%" ``` ::: The biggest variable category: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} category_totals |> dplyr::filter(Category %nin% c(fixed, "Subscriptions")) |> dplyr::slice_max(Total, n = 1) #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> Category Total Share #> #> 1 Groceries 303. 12.6% ``` ::: How to read this result: this statement covers only half a month and one \$2,400 paycheck, but the full month's rent. That is why fixed costs look like 80% of income. Always compare a full month of spending against a full month of income before drawing conclusions. ## Python The same three answers with `polars`: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} income = py_bank_statement.filter(pl.col("Amount") > 0)["Amount"].sum() category_totals = ( py_bank_statement .filter(pl.col("Amount") < 0) .group_by("Category") .agg((-pl.col("Amount").sum()).alias("Total")) .sort("Total", descending=True) .with_columns((pl.col("Total") / income).alias("Share")) ) category_totals ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Excel With `Date` in `A`, `Description` in `B`, `Amount` in `C`, and `Category` in `D`, the [`SUMIF()` function](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/sumif-function) adds up one category. Total spent on subscriptions: ```swift =-SUMIF(D:D, "Subscriptions", C:C) ``` The minus sign turns the negative spending total into a positive number. Fixed costs as a share of income (format the cell as a percentage): ```swift =-(SUMIF(D:D,"Housing",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Utilities",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Insurance",C:C))/SUMIF(C:C,">0") ``` For every category at once, select the data and use **Insert → PivotTable**, with `Category` in Rows and `Amount` in Values. ::: ## The Subscription Audit Math A \$20/month subscription feels trivial. Cancel it and invest the \$240 a year instead, and the chart below shows what that money grows into at each checkpoint, split into the money you put in and the growth it earned. **Formula:** Annual cost × ((1 + r)\^n − 1) ÷ r = Opportunity cost in *n* years With the book's 7% real return (the return after inflation), *r* = 0.07. ::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![$240 a year invested at 7% instead of a $20/month subscription](tracking_spending_files/figure-html/subscription-bar-model-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![$240 a year invested at 7% instead of a $20/month subscription](tracking_spending_files/figure-html/subscription-bar-model-2.png){width=576} ::: ::: Each bar adds another year's \$240 to everything saved so far, and the whole pile grows by 7%. After 30 years you put in \$7,200, and growth added about \$15,500. ::: panel-tabset ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} subscription_opportunity_cost <- function(monthly_cost, years, rate = 0.07) { annual_cost <- monthly_cost * 12 annual_cost * ((1 + rate)^years - 1) / rate } ``` ::: A \$20/month subscription for 30 years at 7%: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost = 20, years = 30) |> fmt_dollar() #> [1] "$22,670.59" ``` ::: Sanity check: money put in vs. growth. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} oc <- subscription_opportunity_cost(20, 30) put_in <- 20 * 12 * 30 c(put_in = put_in, growth = round(oc - put_in)) #> put_in growth #> 7200 15471 ``` ::: Now audit the four subscriptions in the bank statement above. The function is vectorized, so one call prices them all: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} subs <- r_bank_statement |> dplyr::filter(Category == "Subscriptions") |> dplyr::transmute(Description, monthly = -Amount) subs$after_10 <- round(subscription_opportunity_cost(subs$monthly, 10)) subs$after_30 <- round(subscription_opportunity_cost(subs$monthly, 30)) subs |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Description | monthly| after_10| after_30| |:---------------|-------:|--------:|--------:| |Netflix | 15.99| 2651| 18125| |Spotify | 10.99| 1822| 12457| |NYTimes Digital | 17.00| 2819| 19270| |24 Hour Fitness | 39.99| 6630| 45330| ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fmt_dollar(sum(subs$after_30)) #> [1] "$95,182.00" ``` ::: How to read this result: the \$83.97 a month in this statement is a \$95,000 decision over 30 years. The gym membership alone is nearly half of it. The book's survey figure of \$219/month uses monthly deposits. The audit formula above uses yearly deposits, which comes out a little lower: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # yearly deposits (the audit formula) subscription_opportunity_cost(219, 30) |> fmt_dollar() #> [1] "$248,242.95" # monthly deposits (the book's ~$267,000) (219 * ((1 + 0.07 / 12)^(30 * 12) - 1) / (0.07 / 12)) |> fmt_dollar() #> [1] "$267,173.65" ``` ::: Edge case: a rate of 0 divides by zero and returns `NaN`. With no growth, the opportunity cost is just the money you would have spent. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} subscription_opportunity_cost(20, 30, rate = 0) #> [1] NaN 20 * 12 * 30 #> [1] 7200 ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost, years, rate=0.07): annual_cost = monthly_cost * 12 return annual_cost * ((1 + rate) ** years - 1) / rate ``` ::: A \$20/month subscription for 30 years at 7%: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fmt_dollar(subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost=20, years=30)) #> '$22,670.59' ``` ::: Sanity check: money put in vs. growth. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} oc = subscription_opportunity_cost(20, 30) put_in = 20 * 12 * 30 print(fmt_dollar(put_in, 0), fmt_dollar(oc - put_in, 0)) #> $7,200 $15,471 ``` ::: Audit the four subscriptions in the bank statement. `polars` expressions are vectorized, so the formula runs on every row: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} subs = ( py_bank_statement .filter(pl.col("Category") == "Subscriptions") .select("Description", (-pl.col("Amount")).alias("monthly")) .with_columns( subscription_opportunity_cost(pl.col("monthly"), 10).round(0).alias("after_10"), subscription_opportunity_cost(pl.col("monthly"), 30).round(0).alias("after_30"), ) ) subs ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

If the data is arranged differently, adjust the cell references accordingly: ![Opportunity Cost 2 in Excel](img/tracking_spending-opportunity_cost2.png){width='100%' fig-align='center'} ![Opportunity Cost Layouts in Excel](img/tracking_spending-opportunity_cost_layouts.png){width='100%' fig-align='center'} :::
